o: Exactly one operation: reverse a prefix of length k or a suffix of length k, for any 1 ≤ k ≤ n, minimizing lexicographic order. For dcab, reversing the first 3 gives acdb; for abba, reversing the last 3 gives aabb; for zxy, reversing the first 2 gives xzy. Since n ≤ 1000 there are only 2n candidate strings and comparing each costs O(n), so direct enumeration is fully sufficient.
k: There are only 2n candidates: prefix reversals and suffix reversals for every k.
String comparison is O(n), giving O(n^2) total — well within limits.

a.i: Generate every string obtainable by reversing s[:k] or s[n-k:] for k = 1..n and keep the lexicographically smallest. No structure exploitation is needed at this scale.
s: For k from 1 to n: build prefix-reversed candidate s[:k][::-1] + s[k:] and suffix-reversed candidate s[:n-k] + s[n-k:][::-1].
a.t: O(n^2) — 2n candidates, each compared in O(n)

w: This is the intended solution given n ≤ 1000; mention that larger n would need suffix-array/rank tricks. Pitfalls: forgetting k = n (full reversal) and k = 1 (identity is not allowed since exactly one operation is required — though reversing 1 character is the identity, it is permitted). Follow-up: allow multiple operations, or restrict k to a given set.
